newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Islands row fuels anti-Japan uproar on anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Islands row fuels anti-Japan uproar on anniversary.

text.p: Chinese anger over Tokyo's claim to an archipelago in the East China Sea fuelled anti-Japanese protests in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau on Wednesday -- 65 years to the day after Japan's imperial army invaded China.

On the mainland itself, where the state has managed to suppress popular outbursts against Japan, the Communist Party's powerful propaganda machine spoke for many Chinese who openly acknowledge their lingering suspicions of Japan.

"There are still a minority of Japanese who rigidly grasp the corpse of militarism and will not let go, who return evil for good and constantly create disturbances," thundered the ruling party's mouthpiece People's Daily.

Japan has formally claimed sovereignty to what it calls the Senkakus and insists the issue is not open to discussion with China. Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over what it calls the Diaoyus for centuries.

The English-language China Daily was even more explicit in its commentary. "With one hand busily trying to cover their younger generation's eyes from the historic facts, they are using another hand to pull the scab right off the sore," it said.
A cartoon beside the commentary showed two Japanese, one with a rifle and bloody bayonet, standing over a placard proclaiming Tokyo's ownership of the islands.
Beijing nevertheless has pledged a cautious approach to calls for it to send naval forces to the uninhabited but potentially oil-rich islets, saying the situation was "relatively complicated".

A new Chinese nationalism, sparked by the prospect of the end of British colonial rule in Hong Kong in 1997, has erupted in Asia's disparate Chinese communities since Japan renewed its claim to the islands it calls the Senkakus.
The 65th anniversary of Japan's full-blown invasion of northeast China on September 18, 1937, fostered a volatile mix of these neo-nationalist and anti-Japanese emotions.

In Taiwan, hundreds of protesters besieged Tokyo's de facto Taipei embassy, burning Japanese flags and pummelling an effigy of a Japanese soldier but failing to break a police line to storm the office.

"If Japan's government stubbornly thinks it again can use strategies from 65 years ago to humiliate China, this no doubt would be a declaration of war on China's people," they said in a protest letter handed to Japanese officials.

So strong is anti-Japanese feeling in Taiwan that many people question the loyalty of President Lee Teng-hui, who was schooled in Japanese during the island's 1895-1945 occupation by imperial Japan. Some protesters called for Lee's resignation.
Taiwan's provincial government and biggest county have banned public contracts to Japanese firms and citizens groups in Taiwan and Hong Kong are pushing a boycott of Japanese goods.
In Hong Kong, where ire at Japan's past and present actions has spurred more than a week of street marches, September 18 was marked by scattered protest activities and a candlelit vigil.
The date is a painful one in the Chinese collective memory because the invasion of northeast China spurred a 14-year colonisation drive and a string of war atrocities that still haunt older Chinese.
Hong Kong social workers marched on Wednesday to a Japanese school to demand that Japanese children be taught the truth about Japan's militarist past.
Even in sleepy Macau, a Portuguese-ruled gambling outpost that reverts to Chinese rule in 1999, the anniversary and the Diaoyu dispute sparked an outpouring of anti-Japanese feelings.
School bells tolled through the territory across the Pearl River from Hong Kong as thousands of pupils spilled into school yards for lessons on "Japanese militarism and expansionism".

Chinese-language "big character" posters not unlike those seen in China's ultraleftist Cultural Revolution of 1966-76 hung from buildings, demanding that Japan respect China's sovereignty over the Diaoyu islands.
